{{Short description|Mathematics concept}}

In [[mathematics]], especially [[group theory]], the '''Zappa–Szép product''' (also known as the '''Zappa–Rédei–Szép product''', '''general product''', '''knit product''', '''exact factorization''' or '''bicrossed product''') describes a way in which a [[group (mathematics)|group]] can be constructed from two [[subgroup]]s. It is a generalization of the [[direct product of groups|direct]] and [[semidirect product]]s.  It is named after [[Guido Zappa]] (1940) and [[Jenő Szép]] (1950) although it was independently studied by others including B.H. Neumann (1935), G.A. Miller (1935), and J.A. de Séguier (1904).<ref name="LiebeckPraeger2010">{{cite book |authorlink1=Martin Liebeck |author1=Martin W. Liebeck|author2=Cheryl E. Praeger|author3=Jan Saxl|title=Regular Subgroups of Primitive Permutation Groups|year=2010|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-4654-4|pages=1–2}}</ref>

==Internal Zappa–Szép products==

Let ''G'' be a group with [[identity element]] ''e'', and let ''H'' and ''K'' be subgroups of ''G''. The following statements are equivalent:
* ''G'' = ''HK'' and ''H'' ∩ ''K'' = {''e''}
* For each ''g'' in ''G'', there exists a unique ''h'' in ''H'' and a unique ''k'' in ''K'' such that ''g = hk''.
 
If either (and hence both) of these statements hold, then ''G'' is said to be an internal '''Zappa–Szép product''' of ''H'' and ''K''.

==Examples==

Let ''G''  = GL(''n'','''C'''), the [[general linear group]] of [[invertible matrix|invertible]] ''n × n'' [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] over the [[complex number]]s. For each matrix ''A'' in ''G'', the [[QR decomposition]] asserts that there exists a unique [[unitary matrix]] ''Q'' and a unique [[upper triangular matrix]] ''R'' with [[positive number|positive]] [[real number|real]] entries on the main [[Diagonal#Matrices|diagonal]] such that ''A'' = ''QR''. Thus ''G'' is a Zappa–Szép product of the [[unitary group]] ''U''(''n'') and the group (say) ''K'' of upper triangular matrices with positive diagonal entries.

One of the most important examples of this is [[Philip Hall]]'s 1937 theorem on the existence of [[Hall subgroup|Sylow system]]s for [[soluble group]]s.  This shows that every soluble group is a Zappa–Szép product of a Hall ''p<nowiki>'</nowiki>''-subgroup and a Sylow ''p''-subgroup, and in fact that the group is a (multiple factor) Zappa–Szép product of a certain set of representatives of its Sylow subgroups.

In 1935, [[George Abram Miller|George Miller]] showed that any non-regular transitive permutation group with a regular subgroup is a Zappa–Szép product of the regular subgroup and a point stabilizer.  He gives PSL(2,11) and the alternating group of degree 5 as examples, and every alternating group of prime degree is also an example.  This same paper gives a number of examples of groups which cannot be realized as Zappa–Szép products of proper subgroups, such as the quaternion group and the alternating group of degree 6.

==External Zappa–Szép products==

As with the direct and semidirect products, there is an external version of the Zappa–Szép product for groups which are not known ''a priori'' to be subgroups of a given group. To motivate this, let ''G'' = ''HK'' be an internal Zappa–Szép product of subgroups ''H'' and ''K'' of the group ''G''. For each ''k'' in ''K'' and each ''h'' in ''H'', there exist α(''k'', ''h'') in ''H'' and β(''k'', ''h'') in ''K'' such that ''kh'' = α(''k'', ''h'') β(''k'', ''h''). This defines [[map (mathematics)|mappings]] α : ''K'' × ''H'' → ''H'' and β : ''K'' × ''H'' → ''K'' which turn out to have the following properties:

* α(''e'', ''h'') = ''h'' and β(''k'', ''e'') = ''k'' for all ''h'' in ''H'' and ''k'' in ''K''.
* α(''k''<sub>1</sub>''k''<sub>2</sub>, ''h'') = α(''k''<sub>1</sub>, α(''k''<sub>2</sub>, ''h''))
* β(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>''h''<sub>2</sub>) = β(β(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>), ''h''<sub>2</sub>)
* α(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>''h''<sub>2</sub>) = α(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>)α(β(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>), ''h''<sub>2</sub>)
* β(''k''<sub>1</sub>''k''<sub>2</sub>, ''h'') = β(''k''<sub>1</sub>, α(''k''<sub>2</sub>, ''h''))β(''k''<sub>2</sub>, ''h'')

for all ''h''<sub>1</sub>, ''h''<sub>2</sub> in ''H'', ''k''<sub>1</sub>, ''k''<sub>2</sub> in ''K''. From these, it follows that
* For each ''k'' in ''K'', the mapping ''h'' {{mapsto}} α(''k'', ''h'') is a [[bijection]] of ''H''.
* For each ''h'' in ''H'', the mapping ''k'' {{mapsto}} β(''k'', ''h'') is a bijection of ''K''.
(Indeed, suppose α(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>) = α(''k'', ''h''<sub>2</sub>). Then ''h''<sub>1</sub> = α(''k''<sup>−1</sup>''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>) = α(''k''<sup>−1</sup>, α(''k'', ''h''<sub>1</sub>)) = α(''k''<sup>−1</sup>, α(''k'', ''h''<sub>2</sub>)) = ''h''<sub>2</sub>. This establishes injectivity, and for surjectivity, use ''h'' = α(''k'', α(''k''<sup>−1</sup>,''h'')).)

More concisely, the first three properties above assert the mapping α : ''K'' × ''H'' → ''H'' is a [[Group action (mathematics)#Definition|left action]] of ''K'' on (the underlying set of) ''H'' and that β : ''K'' × ''H'' → ''K'' is a [[Group action (mathematics)#Definition|right action]] of ''H'' on (the underlying set of) ''K''. If we denote the left action by ''h'' → <sup>''k''</sup>''h'' and the right action by ''k'' → ''k''<sup>''h''</sup>, then the last two properties amount to <sup>''k''</sup>(''h''<sub>1</sub>''h''<sub>2</sub>) = <sup>''k''</sup>''h''<sub>1</sub> <sup>''k''<sup>''h''<sub>1</sub></sup></sup>''h''<sub>2</sub> and (''k''<sub>1</sub>''k''<sub>2</sub>)<sup>''h''</sup> = ''k''<sub>1</sub><sup><sup>''k''<sub>2</sub></sup>''h''</sup> ''k''<sub>2</sub><sup>''h''</sup>.

Turning this around, suppose ''H'' and ''K'' are groups (and let ''e'' denote each group's identity element) and suppose there exist mappings α : ''K'' × ''H'' → ''H'' and β : ''K'' × ''H'' → ''K'' satisfying the properties above. On the [[cartesian product]] ''H'' × ''K'', define a multiplication and an inversion mapping by, respectively,

* (''h''<sub>1</sub>, ''k''<sub>1</sub>)(''h''<sub>2</sub>, ''k''<sub>2</sub>) = (''h''<sub>1</sub>α(''k''<sub>1</sub>, ''h''<sub>2</sub>), β(''k''<sub>1</sub>, ''h''<sub>2</sub>)''k''<sub>2</sub>)
* (''h'', ''k'')<sup>−1</sup> = (α(''k''<sup>−1</sup>,''h''<sup>−1</sup>), β(''k''<sup>−1</sup>,''h''<sup>−1</sup>))

Then ''H'' × ''K'' is a group called the external '''Zappa–Szép product''' of the groups ''H'' and ''K''. The [[subset]]s ''H'' × {''e''} and {''e''} × ''K'' are subgroups [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to ''H'' and ''K'', respectively, and ''H'' × ''K'' is, in fact, an internal Zappa–Szép product of ''H'' × {''e''} and {''e''} × ''K''.

==Relation to semidirect and direct products==

Let ''G'' = ''HK'' be an internal Zappa–Szép product of subgroups ''H'' and ''K''. If ''H'' is [[normal subgroup|normal]] in ''G'', then the mappings α and β are given by, respectively, α(''k'',''h'') = ''k h k''<sup>&minus; 1</sup> and β(''k'', ''h'') = ''k''. This is easy to see because <math>(h_1k_1)(h_2k_2) = (h_1k_1h_2k_1^{-1})(k_1k_2)</math> and  <math>h_1k_1h_2k_1^{-1}\in H</math> since by normality of <math>H</math>, <math>k_1h_2k_1^{-1}\in H</math>. In this case, ''G'' is an internal semidirect product of ''H'' and ''K''.

If, in addition, ''K'' is normal in ''G'', then α(''k'',''h'') = ''h''. In this case, ''G'' is an internal direct product of ''H'' and ''K''.
